summary: A brick light on a small island at the entrance to Northeast Harbor, Maine: lit 1839, rebuilt 1889, keepers to 1981, now a privately leased station closed to the public.

lens.where: Original fifth-order lens, 1858 (US Lighthouse Society); current optic an acrylic modern optic

structures.note: Attached to a workroom. 31 ft from base to lantern centre (US Lighthouse Society). Earlier towers: wooden tower on a stone house, 1839; a brick tower built 1852-53.
Frame dwelling completed in 1889 at $3,750 (LighthouseFriends); replaced the 1839 stone dwelling.

staffing.note: Keeper roster runs to at least 1981; the light was deactivated that year (LighthouseFriends).

access.note: Privately leased from the National Park Service. Closed to the public. Views from the water by boat or on guided tours.

facts.agency: National Park Service, Acadia National Park (owner; privately leased); US Coast Guard maintains the light as an aid to navigation (per the park)

events.note: Navy Captain Joseph Smith surveyed the coast and urged a light on Bear Island (LighthouseFriends quotes his report).
A $3,000 appropriation granted on July 7, 1838 (LighthouseFriends).
Station established: wooden tower on a stone keeper's house.
Fixed white light from seven lamps with 13-inch reflectors (LighthouseFriends).
Inspector I.W.P. Lewis said one lamp would do instead of seven (LighthouseFriends).
Severely damaged by fire in 1852 (LighthouseFriends).
Brick tower erected off one end of the dwelling (nomination).
Rebuilt with a 31-foot cylindrical brick tower at the southern end of the dwelling (LighthouseFriends).
Fifth-order Fresnel lens (US Lighthouse Society gives 1858; LighthouseFriends gives 1856).
170-foot crib wharf erected (LighthouseFriends); wharf extended later (Lighthouse Board).
Bell tower built on the island; a 1,000-pound bell struck by machinery (LighthouseFriends).
Entire station pulled down and rebuilt; new brick tower and dwelling at $3,750 (nomination; LighthouseFriends).
Storm of March 2, 1900 damaged the wharf (Lighthouse Board).
Keeper Heber G. Sawyer towed a disabled motor boat with his personal launch (Bulletin, April 20).
Keeper's entry in the Commissioner's fiscal 1916 rescue table (printed 'H. O. Sawyer').
Keeper's entry in the Commissioner's fiscal 1918 rescue table (OCR 'H. 0. Sawyer').
Keeper towed a disabled motor launch with one man aboard to port (Commissioner, fiscal 1921).
Passed to the US Coast Guard (LighthouseFriends).
Light deactivated and replaced by two lighted bell buoys offshore (LighthouseFriends).
National Park Service gained ownership of the station (LighthouseFriends).
Listed on the National Register of Historic Places (LighthouseFriends).
Relit by Friends of Acadia as a private aid to navigation, a white flash every five seconds (LighthouseFriends).

notes_for_editor: 1. First keeper: LighthouseFriends says other sources list John G. Bowen as the first keeper and that The Island of Mount Desert Register (1909-10) names William Moore; the story gives both. 2. Lens: the US Lighthouse Society gives a fifth-order Fresnel lens in 1858; LighthouseFriends gives 1856; the story gives both. 3. Tower and station dates: the nomination dates the rebuild to 1889 and its significance statement dates the design to 'the 1870s'; the record's 'built 1839' for the tower is corrected (see corrections). 4. Current light: the park says the Coast Guard maintains the light as an aid to navigation; LighthouseFriends describes a 1989 relight as a private aid; the US Lighthouse Society lists an active private aid. The story says sources differ. The record's 'Fl R 4s' is in no source read; it is not in facts. Check the Coast Guard Light List before publishing it as lit. 5. Focal height: the record's 10.1 m does not match the park (101 ft above the water) or the US Lighthouse Society (100 ft above mean high water); left out of facts. 6. Turner: LighthouseFriends says he transferred to Bear Island from Great Duck Island in the 1930s; the roster has him from 1924 (and again from 1930). 7. Name variants: Caleb L. Gould (LighthouseFriends text: Caleb S. Goold); Larry F. Conley (LighthouseFriends: Larry E. Conley); Edward M. Leighton (LighthouseFriends: Edward Leighton); Clifton F. Olsen (LighthouseFriends: Olsen, Sr.). 8. Steve Loiver: LighthouseFriends prints 'Steve Loiver'; the USLHS roster has Steve Oliver for 1978-1980. The sources do not connect the two, so the story does not link them. The quotation is from a public statement in the LighthouseFriends text. 9. OCR-matched table entries: the fiscal 1916 entry (scan p. 165) prints 'H. O. Sawyer'; the fiscal 1918 entry (scan p. 362) reads 'H. 0. Sawyer' in OCR; the fiscal 1921 prose entry (scan p. 663) reads 'II. G. Sawyer' in OCR. All three were matched by position and read as Heber G. Sawyer, whom the roster has keeping the light 1912-1924. The page images were not read; check the initials on the page image before publishing them. 10. The Bulletin 1914 entry (PDF p. 19) is confirmed by corpus.py page. The Light-House Board volumes for fiscal 1892 (p. 374), 1893 (p. 60), 1894 (p. 725) and 1900 (p. 54) were confirmed by corpus.py page; the fiscal 1893 extension 'commenced June 13, 1893, was completed'. 11. The fiscal 1894 fog-signal distance is printed 'li miles' (OCR) and is not used. 12. The 1875 Newfoundland-dog account rests on LighthouseFriends' reading of an 1875 newspaper; not checked in a newspaper archive. 13. The private lessee and any private residents are not named. The 1983 NRHP nomination carries a 'RECEIVED ... National Park Service JAN 05 1983' stamp; the story's 'received by the Park Service in January 1983' follows it. 14. Living-people rule: the keepers after about 1960 named in the roster (Stanley 1959-1960 is before the cut-off) are named only as the roster or LighthouseFriends prints them; the quotations are public statements.

corrections.why: The standing brick tower dates to 1889; the 1839 structure was a wooden tower on a stone house (LighthouseFriends), replaced in 1852-53 and again in 1889 (nomination; US Lighthouse Society).

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The record's 'active' is kept with the private-aid qualifier: the US Lighthouse Society lists an active private aid; the park says the Coast Guard maintains the light; LighthouseFriends describes the 1989 relight as a private aid after the 1981 deactivation.
Other sources name John G. Bowen first, and a 1909 local history names William Moore; the story records both and does not choose.
